extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic / philosophy (undergraduate or general readers)
extracted.subtask_short: logical classification of names and things
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic criteria for classifying names, the things they denote (feelings, substances, attributes), and distinctions (univocal/æquivocal, relative, metaphorical) relevant to propositions and predication in logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative names (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is relative when, being the name of one thing, its signification cannot be explained but by mentioning another; i.e. the name cannot be employed in discourse so as to have meaning unless the name of some other thing than what it is itself the name of, be either expressed or understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative names only with awareness of the correlative they imply (e.g., father implies a child). Relative names connote relations and often actions or roles relative to other things; failing to supply or understand the correlative renders the name meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal vs. æquivocal application of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal (applied univocally) with respect to all things of which it can be predicated in the same sense; it is æquivocal when predicated of different things in different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ambiguous (æquivocal) words are effectively distinct names that coincide accidentally in sound or spelling (e.g., file meaning a steel instrument vs. file meaning a line of soldiers). Treat æquivocal uses as separate terms to avoid fallacies arising from conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical / metaphorical names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is used analogically or metaphorically when predicated of two things not univocally but in somewhat similar senses, with one sense derivative from the primary (e.g., a 'brilliant light' and a 'brilliant achievement').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason from a metaphorical expression as if it were literal; one common fallacy is treating metaphorical uses as identical with original senses. Track primary vs. derivative senses and avoid illegitimate transfers of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition as subject–predicate structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposition is discourse which affirms or denies something of some other thing; it consists of two names joined by a copula, so proof (the object of logic) presupposes such propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing proof or belief, identify the subject and predicate names and their senses; knowing what names signify is requisite to knowing what can be affirmed or denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an enumeration of existences (categories) as basis of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic requires an account of the kinds of Things that can be predicates or have anything predicated of them; an enumeration (via highest genera or categories) aims to list all classes of namable things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware superficial catalogues (e.g., the Aristotelian Categories) which may be redundant or omit important classes such as feelings or states of consciousness. A useful classification must be comprehensive and avoid repetition under different heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of traditional Categories (redundancy and defectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic list of Categories (substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, where, when, situation, habit) is criticized as a mere catalogue with redundancies, omissions (e.g., sensations, feelings, states of mind), and verbal incongruities (e.g., overlapping between situs/ubi, distinctions not philosophically penetrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting categorical schemes, test for (a) coverage of mental phenomena (sensations, emotions, thoughts), (b) non-repetition of items under multiple headings, and (c) philosophical depth beyond ordinary language distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of concrete names for 'existence' and usage guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete names like 'thing', 'being', 'entity', and 'essence' are ambiguous: by custom they often connote substances rather than mere existence, excluding attributes and feelings; such words have been perverted from their original abstract meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge these ambiguities explicitly; employ whichever term (thing, being, entity, etc.) seems least likely to mislead in context, and do not pretend to adhere rigidly to a single sense if that would leave one unable to express needed ideas. Warn readers about inevitable vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: Feelings / States of consciousness as a primary class
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings or States of Consciousness constitute a principal class of namable things. 'Feeling' is used in a broad sense to include Sensation, Emotion, Thought, and Volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish carefully between (a) sensations (the immediate mental states), (b) thoughts (what passes in the mind, not objects of thought), (c) emotions, and (d) volitions. Avoid conflating sensations with the external objects or with attributes named by ordinary language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensation, object, and attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sensation is distinct from the object causing it and from the attribute ascribed to the object. Language often uses one name to denote sensation and attribute (e.g., 'white' denotes both sensation and quality), which can lead to confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, separate (i) the subjective sensation, (ii) the object (cause) purported to produce it, and (iii) the attributed quality; be mindful that sensations can be conceived without external objects and that ordinary vocabulary may conflate these levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensations and bodily states that produce them
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the sensation itself (a state of mind) from the preceding state of bodily organs (the physical agency producing it). 'Bodily feelings' are those immediately occasioned by bodily states, but philosophically all actual feelings are states of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating sensations as bodily states; recognize that scientific accounts of bodily processes explain physical antecedents, but logical analysis should treat sensations as psychological facts distinct from external physical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception and intuitive belief as states of mind (not central to logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception (recognition of an external object as cause of sensation) may be regarded as an act of belief—an intuitive recognition claiming independence from external evidence; such intuitive beliefs are within the variety of feelings but their laws belong to psychology/metaphysics rather than logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doing logical analysis, treat perceptions/intuitive beliefs as psychological facts (states of mind) and note that the conditions under which intuitive belief is legitimate lie outside logic's immediate scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions and actions (their role in connotation of names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitions (acts of will) are a species of active states of mind; many relative names derive much of their connotation from actions (past, present, possible future) of the beings denoted. An action comprises a volition followed by an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpreting relative or role-denoting names (e.g., sovereign/subject, mortgagor/mortgagee), include the connoted actions and conditional actions (including legal-enforcement consequences). Analyze both the volitional intention and the resultant effect when construing 'action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance vs attribute (grammatical and philosophical notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: School-logicians distinguish substance (self-existent; need not be 'of' something) from attribute (must be 'of' something). This grammatical lesson is inadequate; metaphysicians instead classify substances as Bodies or Minds and seek deeper definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on grammatical tests ('of' vs. not) to separate substances and attributes; probe metaphysical accounts (e.g., body as external cause of sensations, mind as percipient) and be alert to the interdependence of substance and attributes (neither can be coherently conceived entirely without the other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Body (as external cause of sensations) and the epistemic limit
rubrics_metrics.description: A body may be defined as the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations: our conception of objects consists of aggregates/complex ideas of sensations habitualy occurring together. Idealist objections claim 'body' may be only sensations, but most hold belief in an external cause to be intuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the philosophical controversy (idealism vs. realism) but adopt the practical stance that all we know of external objects is our sensations and their order; treat 'body' as a postulated external cause adequate to produce those sensations while recognizing the noumenal/phenomenal distinction and epistemic limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Mind (as unknown percipient of sensations and feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind is defined as the unknown recipient or percipient of sensations and of all our other feelings; it stands in contrast to body conceived as external cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying namable things, include mind as the substratum or locus of states of consciousness; analysis should keep clear the functional distinction (recipient vs. cause) without presuming metaphysical details beyond logical necessity.
